newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan seeks regular summits with ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks regular summits with ASEAN.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is seeking summit meetings with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to enhance ties with the increasingly influential region, a Japanese official said.

The government official, who asked not to be identified, said Indonesian President Suharto would make a summit proposal to fellow members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) when they met in December.

Hashimoto has pushed the idea during visits to five of the seven ASEAN members -- Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore -- and found them "in favour of enhanced contacts at all levels", the official said.
"Suharto was the most supportive. He told us he would be proposing an intensification of top leaders' contacts in December," he told reporters late on Sunday.
Hashimoto arrived in Singapore on Sunday and will leave for home on Tuesday.
"Japan would like to address international issues jointly with the ASEAN countries," the official said. He said there had been no specific proposal on how often an ASEAN-Japan summit should be held.
Japan already participates in annual meetings with ASEAN, along with the United States and the European Union, at the foreign minister level.
ASEAN, home to some of the world's fastest-growing economies and increasingly courted on the diplomatic stage, has not held regular summits with leaders from outside the organisation.
About 16 percent of Japan's total trade is with ASEAN, which also includes the Philippines and Thailand, and Japanese firms are heavy investors in the region.
But Hashimoto's trip, which went ahead even though Marxist rebels still hold 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru, was aimed at moving ties with ASEAN beyond the economic level.
"Going ahead with the visit was a very difficult decision. The decision to go ahead is a measure of the importance Japan attaches to relations with ASEAN," the Japanese official said.
He and other officials have played down suggestions during the tour that Japan wanted to build security relations with ASEAN as a counterweight to the increasing influence of China.
But he said Hashimoto was stressing during his visits that he saw peace and stability in Asia as crucial for Japan's own development as well as the region's.
The keys to stability are a continued U.S. military presence in Asia and "support for China's efforts to participate in the international community as a constructive partner", the official said.
Hashimoto, who visited the Philippines and Thailand last year, had stressed during the current tour that effective cooperation between Japan and ASEAN was vital in preserving stability.
Hashimoto is scheduled to set out his strategic ideas in a major speech in Singapore on Tuesday, shortly before flying back to Tokyo.
The official declined to discuss Hashimoto's speech, saying it had not been completed.
But Singapore analysts said they were looking forward to hearing what Hashimoto had to say.
"Japan is the most potent player in the region and therefore any enhancement of its involvement would be welcome," said one regional analyst, who declined to be identified.
